routines.name: _string_list
routines.docstring:
Return a list of change IDs, or raise invalid-change.

A non-array value or a non-string/empty element is malformed dependency or
journal input (SPEC.md:12); JSON numbers, nulls and nested arrays are all
rejected the same way.

routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Validate change records and fold identical duplicates.

Returns {id, component, units, depends_on} rows with depends_on as a sorted
tuple, i.e. set semantics: dependency order is not identity. Folding happens
here, before graph construction and accounting, so plan and rollback see one
entry per ID. Same ID with a different component/units/dependency set fails
conflicting-change (SPEC.md:11).

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring:
Validate the persisted release journal: already applied change IDs.

Callers pass request.get("applied", []) so an absent field means no prior
release (SPEC.md:5). An explicit null is malformed input and is rejected by
_string_list as invalid-change (SPEC.md:12), the same as any other
non-array; only a missing field gets the empty default.
Unknown IDs are not detectable here because the graph is not built yet;
graph_order raises unknown-dependency for them.

routines.name: _missing_targets
routines.docstring: True when some dependency names an ID absent from the folded graph.

routines.name: graph_order
routines.docstring:
Validate the dependency graph and return the full deterministic order.

Order rule: among currently eligible changes (all dependencies already
emitted) pick the lexicographically smallest ID. heapq over ID strings gives
that tie-break cheaply, and the result does not depend on input order, so
planner.py reuses one order for plan (filtered) and rollback (reversed).

The order is built from every dependency edge, never from
depends_on-minus-applied: applied IDs must still constrain their consumers.
If they were dropped, a consumer and its already applied prerequisite would
become eligible together and only lexical order would decide, so the reverse
used by rollback would put the consumer before its prerequisite and break
SPEC.md:14. `applied` is used here only to validate unknown IDs; plan
filtering and budget accounting happen in planner.py.

Graph errors are raised before returning anything, so a rejected request can
never yield partial actions: a missing dependency target, or an applied ID
absent from the graph, means unknown-dependency; leftover nodes after the
sweep mean a cycle anywhere in the graph, reported as dependency-cycle
(SPEC.md:12).

comments: # type() rather than isinstance: bool is an int subclass and
# SPEC excludes booleans from integer fields.
# Eligible = no unmet dependency at all. Applied changes are ordinary nodes
# here; treating them as pre-satisfied would only matter for plan filtering,
# which planner.py already handles by dropping applied IDs from the output.
journal.py.moduleNote:
Validate, fold and replay release journal records.

This module owns input validation, change identity and replay state. It is
imported only by planner.py (the fixed direction release -> planner ->
journal / policy), so it must not import either of them: graph facts come back
as plain data and every rejection is a JournalError whose message is the exact
SPEC error code.

routines.name: failure
routines.docstring: Exact failure envelope: a rejected request reports no partial actions.

comments: # Fold duplicates before anything is counted or ordered, so identity,
# conflicting-change detection and units accounting all see one row per ID.
# Reverse the full deterministic order first, then keep the applied
# IDs: that is literally SPEC.md:14 and it fixes the positions of the
# emitted subset. Filtering first and reversing afterwards would give
# a different order whenever an unapplied change sorts into the list.
# The success body is built only after every check passed, so a rejected
# operation can never emit a subset of actions.
# Kept under the old name: release.py and any caller already importing plan()
# keep working; the body now handles both actions via the request itself.
planner.py.moduleNote:
Compose policy and journal data into the final result object.

Import direction is fixed: release.py -> planner.py -> journal.py / policy.py.
This module owns assembly only: policy decides whether the request is allowed,
journal owns record identity, replay state and graph order, and the body below
just turns that deterministic order into plan or rollback actions.

routines.name: authorize
routines.docstring:
Check environment and action, then the budget format; return the budget.

Order matters for deterministic error codes: an unknown environment is
reported before an unsupported action, and both before an invalid budget.
The budget is only format-checked here (nonnegative integer, booleans
excluded). Whether it caps the work is a per-action question answered by
admits(), because rollback is not capped in G1.

routines.name: admits
routines.docstring:
True when an action of `units` may run under `budget`.

Only plan spends budget (SPEC.md:13): the caller passes the units actually
emitted after folding and replay, so already applied changes never count.
Rollback is never capped, which is why this is a separate function rather
than a check inside authorize().

comments: # G1 authorizes both environments for plan and rollback (SPEC.md:14). G2-style
# restrictions belong in this table, not in planner.py.
# isinstance(str) is checked before membership: an array or object value is
# unhashable, and `value in set` would raise TypeError and abort the process
# instead of returning the coded error with exit code 0.
policy.py.moduleNote:
Validate release environment, action and budget before computing actions.

Imported only by planner.py (fixed direction release -> planner -> journal /
policy). This module decides what the caller is allowed to request; it never
builds actions, so a rejection here cannot leave partial output behind.

routines.name: read_retain
routines.docstring:
Validate a staging rollback's retain list; return it in request order.

retain is a rollback-only field (CHANGE-G2.md:7): planner.py calls this only
on the rollback path, so a malformed retain on a plan request must never
raise invalid-retain nor change the plan result. The shape rules mirror the
journal (non-array, null, empty string or non-string element) but use their
own code, and a missing field defaults to empty. Membership in `applied` is
not checked here because retain's legal values depend on replay state that
planner.py holds; if it is not an applied ID, planner.py rejects it.

Callers pass request.get("retain", []) so an absent field means nothing is
retained (all applied changes roll back, exactly as in G1). Rejections are
JournalError("invalid-retain") so the request still yields the shared error
envelope instead of partial actions.

Validate, fold and replay release journal records.

routines.name: retained_for
routines.docstring:
Return the applied IDs a rollback must keep (CHANGE-G2.md:7).

The kept set is retain itself plus every prerequisite reachable from it
through the dependency edges, restricted to applied IDs: an already
retained change without its applied prerequisite would be left running on
top of a prerequisite that was just removed. Prerequisites that are not
applied are dropped silently, not reported: they need no protection because
nothing is being rolled back for them, and plan already owns the
"dependency not yet released" question. `depends_on` maps every folded
change to its dependency tuple, i.e. the same full edge set graph_order
used, so retention and ordering cannot disagree about edges.

Membership in `applied_ids` is enforced by the caller before this runs, so
every retain entry is a known node here.

routines.docstring: Exact failure envelope: a rejected request reports no partial actions.

comments: # Fold duplicates before anything is counted or ordered, so identity,
# conflicting-change detection and units accounting all see one row per ID.
# rollback only: plan ignores retain entirely, so a malformed retain
# on a plan request changes nothing (CHANGE-G2.md:7).
# Malformed and not-applied retain entries intentionally share
# invalid-retain: both mean "this rollback cannot be honoured".
# Reverse the full deterministic order first, then keep the applied
# IDs minus the retained ones: that is literally SPEC.md:14 and it
# fixes the positions of the emitted subset. Filtering first and
# reversing afterwards would give a different order whenever an
# unapplied change sorts into the list, and retention must filter
# the same list rather than re-sort it.
# The success body is built only after every check passed, so a rejected
# operation can never emit a subset of actions.
# Kept under the old name: release.py and any caller already importing plan()
# keep working; the body now handles both actions via the request itself.

Compose policy and journal data into the final result object.

routines.name: authorize
routines.docstring:
Check environment and action, then the budget format; return the budget.

Order matters for deterministic error codes: an unknown environment is
reported before an unsupported action, and both before an invalid budget;
a recognised but frozen environment (production) short-circuits all of them
with production-frozen, because the freeze precedes graph and change
validation (CHANGE-G2.md:5).
The budget is only format-checked here (nonnegative integer, booleans
excluded). Whether it caps the work is a per-action question answered by
admits(), because rollback is not capped.

routines.name: admits
routines.docstring:
True when an action of `units` may run under `budget`.

Only plan spends budget (SPEC.md:13): the caller passes the units actually
emitted after folding and replay, so already applied changes never count.
Rollback is never capped, which is why this is a separate function rather
than a check inside authorize().

A staging plan is additionally capped at STAGING_PLAN_LIMIT: the effective
budget is min(request budget, 3), so budget 10 with 4 units of work still
fails while exactly 3 units pass (CHANGE-G2.md:6). authorize() has already
rejected production, so reaching this branch means staging.

comments: # This point release is staging-only (CHANGE-G2.md:5). production stays a
# *recognised* environment so that it is frozen deliberately instead of falling
# through to invalid-environment; eligibility, not recognition, is what G2
# restricts. Environment policy belongs in this table, not in planner.py.
# Ceiling on a staging plan's spending, independent of what the caller allows
# (CHANGE-G2.md:6). It bounds plan only: rollback is a journal-driven undo and
# keeps its G1 rule of a format-checked but uncapped budget (SPEC.md:14).
# isinstance(str) is checked before membership: an array or object value is
# unhashable, and `value in set` would raise TypeError and abort the process
# instead of returning the coded error with exit code 0.
# Frozen before action/budget/changes are examined (CHANGE-G2.md:5
# "before graph or change validation"): the freeze has to win over
# every structural complaint, so a production request with a malformed
# graph, unknown applied ID or bad budget still gets production-frozen
# instead of invalid-change/invalid-budget. Keep this ahead of the
# action and budget checks, and never relocate it into planner.py
# after read_changes(). Both plan and rollback are frozen here.
